title: Geometry-Aware Probabilistic Circuits via Voronoi Tessellations
claim: Adding geometry-aware structure to base models improves density estimation across datasets, with certified lower bounds still often beating the baselines.
layout: 1 wide panel, 8 dataset columns, lollipop stems from zero baseline
description: A single wide lollipop-style chart compares test log-likelihood across eight synthetic 2D and 3D datasets: Alphabet, CheckerBoard, Pinwheel, Spiral, BentLissajous, InterlockedCircles, knotted and TwistedEight. Each dataset column has six stems hanging from or rising off a dashed zero line. Blue marks are EinsumNet and red marks are HCLT. Circles are baselines, squares are the HFV variant and triangles are the VT variant. Baselines and HFV mostly sit near -1 to -2.3, while the VT triangles reach much higher. On several datasets, such as BentLissajous, InterlockedCircles, CheckerBoard and Pinwheel, the triangles rise above zero as tall arrows. A legend sits at the top left, the y-axis is labeled Test Log-Likelihood, and light vertical dividers separate the datasets. The eye goes first to the tall upward triangles.
caption: Mean Test Log-likelihood (↑) on synthetic 2D and 3D density estimation tasks achieved by EinsumNet and HCLT along with their geometry-aware extensions using Voronoi tessellations (VT) and hierarchical factorized Voronoi (HFV), averaged across 3 trials. For VT, values correspond to the lower bound on the log-likelihood obtained via our certified approximate inference framework.
abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) enable exact and tractable inference but employ data independent mixture weights that limit their ability to capture local geometry of the data manifold. We propose Voronoi tessellations (VT) as a natural way to incorporate geometric structure directly into the sum nodes of a PC. However, naÃ¯vely introducing such structure breaks tractability. We formalize this incompatibility and develop two complementary solutions: (1) an approximate inference framework that provides guaranteed lower and upper bounds for inference, and (2) a structural condition for VT under which exact tractable inference is recovered. Finally, we introduce a differentiable relaxation for VT that enables gradient-based learning and empirically validate the resulting approach on standard density estimation tasks.
